nameStory: Sweet cicely gets its name from its wonderfully fragrant, anise-like scent that fills the air when you brush against its leaves or crush them gently. The word 'cicely' comes from 'Seselis,' an ancient Greek name for similar aromatic plants, while 'sweet' refers to the plant's sugary fragrance and taste. It's also called 'myrrh' because early herbalists thought its sweet scent resembled the precious biblical spice.
description: Sweet cicely is a graceful herbaceous perennial that belongs to the carrot family, reaching 2-4 feet tall with delicate, fern-like foliage. This aromatic herb produces clusters of tiny white flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped heads typical of its family. The entire plant has a lovely anise or licorice scent that becomes stronger when the leaves are touched or bruised. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery for nature explorers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, feathery leaves that are finely divided into many small leaflets, creating a delicate fern-like appearance. When crushed, they release a sweet anise or licorice fragrance that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers arranged in flat-topped umbrella clusters (umbels) typical of the carrot family, blooming in late spring to early summer. Each flower head is 2-4 inches across and made up of many tiny individual flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an upright, branching clump 2-4 feet tall and wide, with hollow, ridged stems that feel smooth to the touch. The overall appearance is soft and billowy, almost cloud-like.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, elongated brown seeds about 3/4 inch long with distinct ridges running lengthwise. They're much bigger than most carrot family seeds and turn dark brown to black when ripe.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow, smooth stems with distinctive ridges or grooves running up and down their length. They're typically green with purplish tinges and feel sturdy but not woody.

habitat: Sweet cicely prefers rich, moist soils in partially shaded locations, often found near old gardens, abandoned homesteads, or naturalized around historic properties in New England. It thrives in woodland edges, along stone walls, and in areas with good organic matter in the soil. This European native has escaped cultivation but remains quite uncommon, typically appearing as scattered individual plants rather than large colonies.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh, bright green ferny foliage that's especially fragrant. Young leaves are tender and the sweet anise scent is at its strongest during cool, moist spring weather.
seasonality.summer: White umbrella-shaped flower clusters bloom from late spring through early summer, followed by the development of distinctive large, ridged seeds. The foliage remains lush and aromatic throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen to dark brown or black and may persist on the plant. Leaves begin to yellow and die back, though they may remain somewhat fragrant even as they fade.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving no above-ground trace. The root system remains alive underground, ready to send up new growth in spring.

funFact: Sweet cicely's seeds taste remarkably like green apples mixed with anise, and were historically used as a natural sweetener and breath freshener - medieval people would chew them after meals like we might use mints today!
confusionNotes: Sweet cicely can be confused with other white-flowered carrot family plants like Queen Anne's lace or poison hemlock, but its distinctive sweet anise fragrance when crushed is a dead giveaway - neither of those smells pleasant! Remember: 'Sweet scent means sweet cicely' - if it doesn't smell like licorice candy, keep looking.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'myrrh,' sweet cicely has no relation to the biblical myrrh, which comes from a completely different plant family. Early herbalists simply borrowed the name because of the plant's sweet, spicy fragrance that reminded them of precious spices from distant lands.
compareHints: Sweet cicely is the only species in its genus Myrrhis, making it unique among New England's carrot family plants. Compared to other white-flowered members of this family, it stands out with its much larger seeds, distinctly sweet anise fragrance, and softer, more delicate foliage texture. While Queen Anne's lace has a carrot-like scent and poison hemlock smells musty and unpleasant, only sweet cicely smells like a delicious anise cookie.
